text: Every control in this chapter so far has protected one resource or one connection. This lesson zooms out to the whole network: if everything can reach everything, compromising a single VM gives an attacker a clear path to everything else. Blast radius is the honest way to frame that — not whether something goes wrong, but how much else it reaches when it does.

Azure's standard answer is hub-spoke: a hub VNet holding shared services like Azure Firewall and a VPN gateway, with each workload or environment peered to it as its own spoke. The part people get wrong is assuming peering alone forces spoke traffic through the hub's firewall — it doesn't. Peering only connects the two VNets you pair directly. Actually routing spoke traffic through a central chokepoint takes a user-defined route on each spoke sending outbound traffic to the firewall's private IP; without it, a spoke only reaches what it's directly peered to.

AWS reaches the same place differently. Rather than one large VPC with subnets, the pattern is separate VPCs per workload, each isolated by default. For more than a handful of them, VPC peering stops working as a hub-spoke mechanism, because peering doesn't transit — if A peers to B and B peers to C, A still can't reach C — and every pair needs its own connection. A Transit Gateway solves that: VPCs attach to one central hub, and its route tables decide exactly which attachments can reach which others.

The clean version of that design routes every spoke VPC only to a shared inspection VPC, often running Network Firewall, and never spoke-to-spoke directly — the same forced-chokepoint idea as Azure's hub-spoke, just built on Transit Gateway route tables instead of UDRs and VNet peering.

Network segmentation alone still has a ceiling. The strongest containment boundary in either cloud isn't network at all — it's a separate AWS account or Azure subscription. A compromised credential or role in one generally can't touch resources in another by default, because IAM and RBAC trust don't cross that boundary, regardless of how the networks are connected. That's why AWS Organizations with per-workload accounts, and Azure management groups over separate subscriptions, sit above network design as the top tier of blast-radius containment.

That closes out network security across both clouds. Chapter 5 moves into the tooling that watches what gets through anyway — Microsoft Defender for Cloud, AWS Security Hub, and GuardDuty — and how to triage what they surface without drowning in noise.
